title: Choosing your service list and checking local demand
audience: Handyman owners planning their first services, or reviewing a service list that has grown too broad
learningOutcomes: Sort each planned service into own-trade work, referral work or out of scope, with a stated reason.
Check local demand and competitor offers using at least five dated sources, and record what the checks showed.
Write a one-page service list in plain customer language that contains no unverified claims.

instruction.heading: Why a narrow service list helps
instruction.body: A service list that says the business will fix anything tends to attract vague enquiries, and it makes it harder for a customer to picture what will happen when they call. A shorter list of specific jobs, named in the words customers actually type into a search box, lets people judge quickly whether the business is the right one for them. Start by writing down every task you have done well in the last few years, paid or unpaid. Then sort the list. Some tasks sit in a clear category, such as hanging doors or patching plasterboard. Others touch licensed trades, such as new power points, gas appliances or plumbing connections. Put those in a separate column marked referral, because a licensed tradesperson does that work, not the handyman. Keep the own-trade column to tasks you can repeat to a good standard.

instruction.heading: Testing whether people want the work
instruction.body: Demand means that people in your area are looking for the work and are willing to pay someone to do it. Check it with at least five local sources: search results for each service in your suburb or town, local community groups, public job-posting sites, noticeboards that property managers and body corporates publish, and conversations with other local tradespeople. Count how often each service appears, and note whether the requests come from homeowners, landlords, agents or strata managers. A service that appears repeatedly and comes from several types of client is worth testing. A service that nobody asks for is not worth advertising yet, however well you can perform it. Write down the date of each check, so the record stays honest when conditions change.

instruction.heading: Studying competitors without copying them
instruction.body: Look at eight to ten local operators who offer work similar to yours. For each one, record the services listed, the way each service is described, whether they quote by the hour, by the job or with a call-out fee, the reviews they show, and any licence or insurance claims they make. Treat each claim as something to verify, not as a fact to repeat. Do not reuse their wording, their prices or their photos. The aim is to find gaps: a service that nobody describes clearly, a suburb nobody covers, or a concern customers have that the competitors do not answer, such as clear written quotes or a site visit within a set number of days. Gaps are where a new business can be useful, provided it can deliver what it promises.

instruction.heading: Deciding on the result
instruction.body: Bring the evidence together on one page. Show the services you will offer, the services you will refer, the places you will work, the demand you found and the gaps you plan to address. If the evidence shows that every service you offer is crowded, narrow the list to one or two specialities, widen the area you serve, or change the mix. Revisit the page after three months of real enquiries. A decision made from a single search is weak evidence, and a list that changes every week means the evidence is not yet clear enough to act on.

procedure: Write down every task you have completed well, paid or unpaid, over the last few years.
Sort each task as own-trade work, referral work or out of scope, and check each referral item against “Scope, consent and trade boundaries”.
Search for each own-trade service in the local area, and record how often it appears and who posts it.
Review eight to ten local competitors, and record their services, pricing method, reviews and claims.
Identify two or three gaps where your skills and local demand overlap.
Write a one-page service list in plain customer language, and record the date of each check.

workedExamples.situation: A handyman has been asked by a customer to install a new power point. The owner has swapped a few light fittings in the past and wants to add electrical work to the public list.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should electrical installation appear on the service list as an own-trade service?
workedExamples.reasoning: Installing or altering fixed electrical wiring is licensed electrical work in Australia, so it cannot appear as own-trade work on the list. The owner can list it as a referral to a licensed electrician, and can state that the business refers the work rather than performs it. Whether any fixture swap is allowed depends on the state or territory rules recorded in “Electrical boundaries and referral”, and those rules must be checked before any task is listed.

equipmentAndPpe: Notebook or spreadsheet for the service sort
Phone or computer for local searches, with dated screenshots kept in the business file
Competitor list with the web address and the check date for each entry

commonErrors.error: Listing every skill, including licensed work, so that a customer cannot tell what the business actually does.
commonErrors.prevention: Sort every item into own-trade, referral or out of scope before writing the public list.

commonErrors.error: Copying a competitor's service names, prices or photos.
commonErrors.prevention: Use your own service names and photos of your own completed work, with the client's consent where a client appears.

commonErrors.error: Deciding that demand exists after one search.
commonErrors.prevention: Check at least five sources on separate days, and record the count and the date for each.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Listing a service is not permission to perform it. Electrical, gas and plumbing work is licensed in each state and territory, and the state rules decide what a handyman may do. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to perform regulated work.
Competitor licence and insurance claims must be checked with the regulator or the insurer before they are repeated. Nothing in this lesson confirms the status of any competitor.

qualityStandard: Every listed service is marked own-trade, referral or out of scope, and the reason is recorded.
At least five dated local demand sources and eight to ten competitors are recorded.
The one-page service list uses plain customer language and contains no licence or insurance claim the owner cannot evidence.
documentationEvidence: Dated service sort with the three categories and the reason for each item
Demand check log with the sources, dates and counts
Competitor review table with services, pricing method and claims marked for verification
summary: Narrow the list to specific services the business can deliver safely.
Refer licensed work, and record the referral as a referral rather than a service.
Base the decision on dated local evidence of demand and gaps, not on one search.

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer asks for a new power point to be installed. What should the service list show?
options: Electrical installation as an own-trade service
A referral to a licensed electrician, with the referral recorded
Nothing, because customers will not search for it
Electrical installation as own-trade work if fixture swaps have been done before

knowledgeChecks.question: Which evidence best shows that local demand exists for a service?
options: The owner's belief that the service is needed and the friends who agree with it
One search result that matches the owner's skills and nothing else
Dated checks across several local sources that show repeated requests
The number of competitors listed on one website and their prices

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the main value of reviewing competitors?
options: Copying their service names and their prices and their advertising slogans and photos
Finding gaps where the owner's skills and local demand meet, without copying their wording
Confirming their licence status on their behalf and checking their insurance policy
Setting the owner's prices from their advertised rates alone for every job in the area
